name: DreamBox Math
line: DreamBox is a K-8 supplement built on discovery. AMP runs through precalculus and explains every answer.
description: AMP vs DreamBox Math: what DreamBox's randomized trials found, where the K-8 supplement stops, and how AMP explains every answer through precalculus.
verdict: DreamBox Math has randomized evidence in the early grades and a hands-on way of building number sense [16][15]. It is a K-8 supplement meant for about an hour a week, and in Harvard's study few students reached the dose DreamBox recommended [1][3][18]. AMP is one program from counting through precalculus that teaches every problem type, explains every answer, schedules review and prints workbooks.

reasons.title: One program from counting through precalculus
reasons.body: DreamBox Math covers kindergarten through grade 8 [2]. Its own help center calls it "a supplemental digital product", meant to support a core curriculum [3]. AMP runs from counting through precalculus on one map of 336 skills, with a lesson for every problem type. A learner who finishes grade 8 math keeps going in the same place.

reasons.title: Every problem comes with its lesson and worked answer
reasons.body: DreamBox teaches through exploration first and puts explicit instruction after it, inside the lesson [3]. When a struggle stops being productive, it says it will show the student how to do it [7]. We found no stand-alone written lesson or worked example for each type of problem in its help center or product pages. Common Sense Media's review says its items can focus more on practice than on instruction, and that children may want more explanation of some concepts [23]. Every one of AMP's 1,384 problem types has a one-step hint and a written lesson with a worked example, and every answer is followed by the correct answer and worked steps. Across 55 studies, worked examples improved math performance by g = 0.48 on average [25].

reasons.title: Help inside AMP never counts as mastery
reasons.body: DreamBox's help center asks adults not to help beyond coaching, because the engine would then adapt to the adult's understanding instead of the child's [7]. AMP builds help in. A hint gives the first step and never the answer, and every reference lesson carries a guide for the parent. An answer given after a hint or the lesson is recorded as helped, and it does not move the level or count toward mastery.

reasons.title: A mastery rule anyone can read
reasons.body: We found no numeric mastery rule in DreamBox's help center or product pages [3][9]. In the Arizona study DreamBox commissioned, lessons counted as completed whether the student passed or failed them [19]. AMP calls a skill Strong only when four of the last five answers are right without help, and the rule sits in public code. Two misses in a row send practice back to what the skill builds on.

reasons.title: Old skills come back on a schedule
reasons.body: DreamBox returns to material when the engine sees a struggle, and resets the lesson so the student replays it [5]. We found no time-based review of skills already learned in its help center or product pages [3][5]. AMP brings each learned skill back after 6 hours, 1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks and a month, mixed with other topics. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [24].

reasons.title: It runs on a phone or an Android tablet
reasons.body: DreamBox's pricing page says it is not available on smartphones or Android tablets [1]. Its help center says it has no Android app, is not optimized for phones, and offers no technical support on Android devices [14]. AMP runs in any current browser on a phone, tablet or computer. It has no app-store app.

reasons.title: Paper is part of the plan
reasons.body: DreamBox Math has no printable worksheets, and its help center says "We do not encourage students to use pencil and paper" while they play lessons [3]. AMP prints unlimited workbooks made for each learner, each with a worked answer key. Results entered from paper count toward the learner's level, so a day off screen still counts.

rows.price: Home: $99.95 a year or $12.95 a month for one child; $149.95 a year or $19.95 a month for a family plan [1]. Schools: no published price [2].
rows.buyers: Families directly, with a 14-day free trial [1]. Schools and districts through a demo request [2].
rows.range: Kindergarten through grade 8 [2]. Its maker describes it as a supplement to a core curriculum [3].
rows.start: At home, the child starts in the upcoming grade and the engine adjusts [8]. Schools can switch on Launchpad, a placement assessment at the start of each school year [9].
rows.teaching: Lessons worked with virtual manipulatives, with narrated directions and hints [15][12]. Explicit instruction comes after exploration [3]. No written lesson per problem type found.
rows.next: The engine picks the next lesson from how the child worked inside the last one. Adults can steer with Assignments [4].
rows.mastery: No numeric mastery rule found. A struggle on a concept resets that lesson's progress so it is replayed [5].
rows.review: No scheduled review found. Material returns when the engine sees a struggle, or when an adult assigns a review topic [5][8].
rows.print: No printable worksheets. DreamBox discourages pencil and paper during lessons [3].
rows.adult: Little to do. Adults are asked not to help beyond coaching, because help skews the engine [7].
rows.reports: A family dashboard: minutes and lessons per week against a five-lesson target, proficiency by standard, and lesson groups that may need attention [10].
rows.evidence: Rated Strong by Evidence for ESSA: two randomized studies, average +0.10, grades K-5 [16]. What Works Clearinghouse: potentially positive effects, grades K-1 (2013) [17].

theirs: DreamBox Math is an adaptive online math program for kindergarten through grade 8, made by Discovery Education [2]. Schools request a demo; no school price is published [2]. Families can subscribe at dreambox.com by the month, the half year, the year, or for a 10-year term [1].

A student signs in to one of three learning environments: one for grades K-2, one for 3-5 and one for 6-8 [6][12]. In a lesson, the child solves problems by working virtual manipulatives such as a math rack, a ten frame, a number line and bar models [15]. Directions and hints are narrated [12]. The engine watches how the child works, not only whether the answer is right, and adjusts difficulty, scaffolding, hints and pacing [3]. In grades 3-8, students collect coins to spend on avatars, music and wallpapers, unlock mini-games, and track a fixed goal of five lessons a week [6].
DreamBox sells home use as about an hour a week [1]. It is built to support a main curriculum, not to replace one [3].
credit: Randomized evidence: Evidence for ESSA rates DreamBox Math Strong, and the What Works Clearinghouse found potentially positive effects in kindergarten and first grade [16][17].

Hands-on models. Children build number sense with virtual manipulatives, and the engine adapts to the strategies they use, not only to the final answer [3][15]. AMP has a few built models, not a full set of manipulatives.
Spanish in every learning environment, and narrated directions and hints [11][12]. AMP is in English only and does not read problems aloud.
A lower price: $99.95 a year for one child, or $149.95 a year for a family plan [1]. AMP costs $599 a year for the first child.
Coins, avatars and mini-games for children who like them, and an iPad app [6][13]. AMP has no games and no app-store app.

theirs: DreamBox has randomized evidence, which many math programs lack. Evidence for ESSA rates DreamBox Math Strong, on two randomized studies with 13,320 students in grades K-5 and an average effect of +0.10 [16]. The What Works Clearinghouse found potentially positive effects in 2013 from one study: SRI International's randomized trial with 557 kindergarten and first-grade students at three Rocketship charter schools. Students who used DreamBox scored 0.11 standard deviations higher on the MAP math test than the comparison group, an improvement index of 4 percentile points [17].

The larger randomized study, by Lenard and Rhea (2019) in 24 North Carolina schools, found +0.12 on a number test in grades K-2 and +0.03 on the state test in grades 4-5 [16]. A 2024 randomized trial that compared DreamBox with Zearn among 115 kindergarten and first-grade students found results favoring DreamBox that were not statistically significant [22]. The measured effects are positive and small, and the clearest ones are in kindergarten through grade 2.

Use falls short of the dose. A 2016 Harvard study of Howard County schools and Rocketship charter schools, funded by a private gift, found students averaged 35 and 44 minutes a week, in the weeks they used it, when DreamBox recommended 60 to 90 [18]. Only 5.8% and 12.5% reached the recommended time. In Howard County, students who used DreamBox the average amount gained about 2 percentile points on MAP over similar non-users, and the authors could not rule out other causes [18].

DreamBox's newer studies were commissioned by DreamBox or Discovery Education, and most compare heavy users with light users. LearnPlatform's 2023 Arizona study found 0.12 for grade 7-8 users against weighted non-users; in grades K-6 fewer than 5% of students were non-users, so only amounts of use could be compared, and 11% averaged more than 5.5 lessons a week [19]. Its 2024 North Carolina study had no non-user group; 25% of students in grades K-2 and 11% in grades 3-5 did more than five lessons a week [20]. McREL's 2025 South Carolina study found that any use of DreamBox alone did not raise average school-level math scores, while schools with consistent use did score higher [21].
ours: Two findings bear on the main differences between DreamBox and AMP. Mixed, spaced review: in a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed practice scored 62% against 38% for practice in blocks, on the researchers' own test a month later [24]. Worked examples: across 55 studies they raised math performance by an average of g = 0.48 [25]. AMP schedules the first and attaches the second to every problem type. We expect that to show in outcomes, and we have committed in public to measuring it.

AMP is new, and its own outcome studies have not run yet. They begin in 2027: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. Until then, the research behind each part of AMP is laid out in our report, and the code is public.

them: Your child is in kindergarten through grade 5 and you want a lower-cost, game-like supplement beside the math you already teach.
Your child learns in Spanish or needs directions read aloud.
Your child loves hands-on models, coins and avatars, and your family uses an iPad.
You run a school that must buy a program rated Strong by Evidence for ESSA.
amp: You want one program for all of math, from counting through precalculus, not an hour-a-week supplement.
You want a lesson with a worked example for every problem, and the worked answer after every one.
You want hints and lessons you can lean on together, with a parent guide in every reference lesson, and helped answers kept out of mastery.
You want old skills to come back on a schedule, and workbooks for days off screen.
Your family uses phones or Android tablets.

questions.question: Is AMP more expensive than DreamBox Math?
questions.answer: Yes. DreamBox Math costs $99.95 a year for one child or $149.95 a year for a family plan, with monthly plans at $12.95 and $19.95 [1]. AMP costs $599 a year or $59 a month for the first child and $399 a year or $39 a month for each additional child, and the account holder and a second parent practice free. The price buys one program from counting through precalculus, a lesson for every problem type, scheduled review and unlimited personalized workbooks.

questions.question: Does DreamBox Math work?
questions.answer: Its randomized studies found small positive effects in the early grades: +0.11 and +0.12 in kindergarten through grade 2 [16][17]. The one randomized test in grades 4-5 found +0.03 on the state test [16]. In Harvard's study, few students used it as much as DreamBox recommended [18].

questions.question: What comes after DreamBox Math?
questions.answer: DreamBox Math ends at grade 8 [2]. AMP continues through Algebra 1, Geometry, Algebra 2 and Precalculus, and places the learner within the first 24 problems and keeps a level in each part of math, with no separate test.

questions.question: Can homeschoolers buy DreamBox Math?
questions.answer: Yes. DreamBox sells home plans for one child or a family, with a 14-day free trial [1]. Its help center suggests starting a child in the upcoming grade level [8].
